# Linear regression with a single continuous predictor {#sec-linear-regression-single-continuous}

```{r}
#| include: false

library(ggplot2)
library(here)

Plot_theme <- source("functions/plot_theme.R")
Plot_theme <- Plot_theme$value

cell_data <- read.csv(here("project/AnalysisData/Cells_Gfap-Pdgfrb.csv"))
cell_data$DPI <- as.numeric(cell_data$DPI)
```

@sec-linear-regression-assumptions left us with a diagnosis and a plan, not a finished model. The straight line across the full 0–30 DPI range of `cell_data` failed linearity and homoscedasticity for a real, biological reason: an early bump from acute edema, then a decline as neurodegeneration takes over, that no single slope can honestly summarize. The plan was to restrict the range to where a straight line is actually a defensible description of the biology, then take that narrower model all the way through: fit it, check it, interpret it, and say what it tells us about the effect of time on tissue after ischemia. That's this chapter.

## The full range, once more

Here's `Tissue_Area` (hemispheric tissue area) against `DPI` again, this time with marginal density plots attached so we can also see how each variable is distributed on its own, not just how they relate.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cell_data_hemisphere_scatter
#| fig-cap: Tissue area against days post-ischemia, full range
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 5
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: false

library(ggExtra)

Area_scatter <- ggplot(
  data = cell_data,
  aes(x = DPI, y = Tissue_Area)
) +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, color = "black", fill = "#56B4E9", se = TRUE) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 7, 14, 30)) +
  labs(x = "Days post-ischemia (DPI)", y = "Tissue area (mm²)") +
  Plot_theme

Area_scatter_Marginal <- ggMarginal(
  Area_scatter,
  type = "densigram",
  colour = "black",
  fill = "#56B4E9",
  alpha = .9
)

Area_scatter_Marginal
```

This is the same picture @sec-linear-regression-assumptions used to diagnose the problem, and the same conclusion holds: a single straight line, drawn across the entire 30-day window, splits the difference between an early rise and a later fall instead of honestly describing either. That's not a flaw specific to this dataset; it's what happens whenever a biological process changes character partway through the timeline you're modeling, and cerebral ischemia's inflammation-then-degeneration arc does exactly that. So we do what the last chapter's diagnostics recommended: narrow the window to a stretch where the biology is closer to monotonic, and model that stretch honestly instead of the whole thing dishonestly.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cell_data_sub_tbl
#| tbl-cap: Cell data table subset (DPI 3, 7, 14)

library(gt)
cell_data_sub <- subset(cell_data, DPI %in% c(3, 7, 14))
gt(head(cell_data_sub))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-cell_data_sub_hemisphere_scatter
#| fig-cap: Tissue area against days post-ischemia, DPI 3-14 subset
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 5
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: false
#| echo: false

Area_sub_scatter <- ggplot(
  data = cell_data_sub,
  aes(x = DPI, y = Tissue_Area)
) +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, color = "black", fill = "#56B4E9", se = TRUE) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(3, 7, 14)) +
  labs(x = "Days post-ischemia (DPI)", y = "Tissue area (mm²)") +
  Plot_theme

Area_sub_scatter_Marginal <- ggMarginal(
  Area_sub_scatter,
  type = "densigram",
  colour = "black",
  fill = "#56B4E9",
  alpha = .9
)

Area_sub_scatter_Marginal
```

Restricted to DPI 3–14, the decline looks far closer to a straight line than the full-range version did, which is exactly the point of subsetting: not to make the data prettier, but to only ask a linear model a question it can honestly answer. Notice, too, that day 3 still shows a noticeably wider spread of points than day 7 or 14: the same acute-phase variability @sec-linear-regression-assumptions flagged in the full dataset hasn't disappeared just because we narrowed the range. Keep that in mind; it's going to matter again in a moment.

::: callout-tip
### Why this subset, and not a wider or narrower one

DPI 3–14 isn't an arbitrary trim; it's the stretch where the biology is doing one thing (degeneration) instead of two (edema, then degeneration). A narrower window would waste data without buying anything; a wider one, reaching back toward day 0 or out toward day 30, would drag the edema bump or the later plateau back into a model that can't represent either.
:::

## Fitting the model

Running this regression answers the same question this book keeps coming back to:

::: {style="text-align: center"}
***What's the value of knowing A if I know B?***
:::

Here, knowing $B$ = days since ischemia, how much does that tell us about $A$ = hemispheric tissue area? The model takes the now-familiar shape:

$$
\text{Area}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{DPI}_i + \epsilon_i, \quad \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)
$$

$\text{Area}_i$ is the tissue area for animal $i$, and $\text{DPI}_i$ its measurement day, both real, numeric, continuous variables, unlike the categorical `Condition` from @sec-intro-applied-modeling. $\beta_0$ is still the intercept: the area the model predicts at $\text{DPI} = 0$, even though day 0 isn't actually in this subset anymore; the model will happily extrapolate an intercept for it regardless, which is worth remembering before you lean on that number too hard. $\beta_1$ is the slope: how much tissue area changes per additional day within this window. And $\epsilon_i$ is everything else, same as always.

```{r}
library(brms)

brms_model <- brm(
  Tissue_Area ~ DPI,
  data = cell_data_sub,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/linear-regression-single-continuous_fit1.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

We haven't specified any priors here: same deliberate choice as @sec-intro-applied-modeling's first model, so the coefficients below reflect the data with as little of our own opinion mixed in as `brms`'s defaults allow. @sec-priors-regularization is where we stop doing that on purpose.

::: panel-tabset
### brms

```{r}
summary(brms_model)
```

Rhat is 1.00 or 1.01 for every parameter, both bulk and tail effective sample sizes clear 2,200 (comfortably past the 400 minimum), and there's no divergent-transition warning, a fit worth trusting on the sampling side, which is a separate question from whether the *model* itself is a good description of the biology (more on that shortly).

### parsnip

```{r}
library(parsnip)
library(broom)

parsnip_model <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(Tissue_Area ~ DPI, data = cell_data_sub)

tidy(parsnip_model, conf.int = TRUE)
```
:::

## Reading the coefficients

Both fits agree closely: an intercept around 18.8 mm² and a `DPI` slope around $-0.67$ mm² per day, with `brms`'s 95% credible interval (roughly $-0.83$ to $-0.52$) and `parsnip`'s 95% confidence interval (roughly $-0.81$ to $-0.53$) both sitting comfortably away from zero. Concretely, that slope says tissue area falls by about 0.67 mm² for every additional day in this window: predicted area drops from around 16.8 mm² at day 3 to around 9.4 mm² by day 14, a decline of roughly 44% over eleven days.

::: callout-warning
### Before you trust this too far

Subsetting fixed the problem it was meant to fix (linearity), but it didn't fix everything. A quick residual check on this exact model shows the same day-3 excess variability we just saw in @fig-cell_data_sub_hemisphere_scatter carrying through into the residuals, and a Shapiro-Wilk test flags the resulting residual distribution as non-normal ($W = 0.88$, $p = 0.002$), driven by that same wider spread at the acute timepoint. With only 31 animals across three groups, chasing this further with a transformation would cost more in interpretability than it would buy in normality, and @sec-beta-robust-regression gives us purpose-built machinery (robust, heavier-tailed likelihoods) for exactly this shape of problem later in the book. File this under "known, honest limitation," not "fatal flaw": the effect direction and its distance from zero are not in question, but the precision quoted above is probably a little optimistic.
:::

Let's actually look at the posterior for that slope, rather than just quoting its interval.

```{r}
#| label: fig-single_continuous_posterior_halfeye
#| fig-cap: Posterior distribution for the DPI slope on tissue area
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.5

library(ggdist)
library(posterior)

draws <- as_draws_df(brms_model)

ggplot(draws, aes(x = b_DPI, y = 0)) +
  stat_halfeye(.width = c(0.5, 0.95), fill = "#0072B2", point_interval = "median_qi") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Posterior for the DPI slope on tissue area", y = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank())
```

The whole mass of that distribution sits well below zero: every plausible value for the slope, weighted by how well it fits what we observed, points the same direction. That's the Bayesian answer to "how sure are we?", in the same sense @sec-intro-applied-modeling walked through in detail: a direct probability statement about the effect itself, not a long-run frequency claim about a procedure.

::: callout-tip
### Frequentist equivalent

`brms` and `lm` land on nearly identical numbers again, for the same reason as in @sec-intro-applied-modeling: with a flat prior, the posterior is shaped almost entirely by the likelihood, which is exactly what `lm` maximizes on its own [@gelman2020]. Thirty-one animals is a small sample by most standards, but it's enough here for the two approaches to agree; the divergence you'll start to see later in the book shows up with hierarchical structure or genuinely uninformative small samples, neither of which applies yet to this single-level model.
:::

## Does the model's story match the data?

@sec-mcmc-model-checking introduced the posterior predictive check as the way to ask whether a fitted model's simulated data actually resembles the real thing, rather than just trusting the coefficients on faith. Let's finally put that to use on a model with something at stake.

```{r}
#| label: fig-single_continuous_ppcheck
#| fig-cap: Posterior predictive check for the DPI model of tissue area
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4

pp_check(brms_model, ndraws = 50)
```

The replicated datasets (light lines) bracket the observed data (dark line) reasonably well: same center, same overall spread, no replicate wildly off from reality. Look closely, though, and the observed curve has a faint two-humped shape that no single replicate quite reproduces: a small echo of the fact that this "one" dataset is really three DPI groups stitched together, one of them (day 3) wider than the other two. A single Gaussian likelihood, by construction, can only ever propose one smooth hump; it has no way to represent "three groups with different spreads" as anything other than an approximation. That's the same day-3 variability from the callout above, showing up here a second way rather than as a new problem. A model doesn't have to be flawless to be useful; it has to be useful in a way you can name precisely, and now we can.

Two coefficients, an honestly-scoped range, a checked fit, and a named limitation: that's a complete linear regression, start to finish. @sec-linear-regression-multiple picks up the natural next question: what happens once we bring a second predictor into this same model? And further out, @sec-longitudinal-timeseries returns to the *entire* 0–30 DPI range we set aside at the start of this chapter, this time with a model built to actually represent a rise followed by a fall, instead of subsetting the problem away.
